description:
Sachatellite — from Kichwa Sacha, meaning "Forest".

We are a university community made up of students from ESPE, UCE and EPN, three public universities in Ecuador. We created Sachatellite knowing that a chart cannot put out a fire. What it can do, however, is provide those who fight them with a clearer picture of wildfire activity through the integration and harmonization of satellite data.
Public data. Science in the service of humanity.
summary:
Sachatellite is a web application that helps firefighters, land managers, and scientists explore historical burning activity using NASA FIRMS observations from MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m). The MODIS record begins in 2000, and the VIIRS record begins in 2012.

Users can select a country or define an area by coordinates, choose a date range, and explore an interactive monthly burning activity calendar and a year-by-year fire footprint. Sachatellite addresses the challenge by expressing each sensor’s monthly activity as a percentage above or below its own historical median for the same calendar month. This lets users see when MODIS and VIIRS both indicate unusually high or low activity in the selected area. Users can also export the selected monthly data as a CSV file.

By showing when burning activity typically peaks and when it departs from historical patterns, Sachatellite helps local teams prioritize monitoring and prepare for periods of elevated fire activity.
details:
Sachatellite is a web application that turns historical NASA FIRMS active fire observations into an interactive burning activity calendar. Users can select a country or define an area by coordinates, choose a date range, and explore monthly activity through a calendar, a year-by-year fire footprint, and a map with month-by-month playback. They can also export the selected monthly data as a CSV file for further analysis.

The application measures burning activity in active cell-days. A grid cell counts once per day when it contains at least one valid detection, even if the sensor records several hotspots that day. MODIS and VIIRS differ in spatial resolution and observation coverage, so Sachatellite puts their monthly activity on a common scale. It expresses each sensor’s activity as a percentage above or below its own historical median for the same calendar month. The comparison view overlays those two series for their shared observation period, while the calendar preserves the activity values for each sensor.

The project’s creative contribution is turning those observations into a practical question for users: When should we pay closer attention? A dedicated panel highlights the months that have historically been most active and recent months that exceeded previous records. Our intended impact is to make satellite observations easier to use in local preparedness. Firefighters and land managers can use the historical patterns to decide when to intensify monitoring, and researchers can use the exported data to investigate unusual periods in more detail.

In designing the analysis, we considered seasonal variation, differences between sensors, and how to handle missing observations, partial months, and historical medians of zero. The default view focuses on presumed vegetation fires, with an option to include volcanoes and other thermal sources. We built the interface in React and TypeScript with Vite, and used Node.js to process NASA FIRMS records into monthly aggregates and map data that the app loads as JSON. The interface is available in English and Spanish.

Our team brings together members of three public universities in Ecuador: Universidad de las Fuerzas Armadas ESPE, Escuela Politécnica Nacional (EPN), and Universidad Central del Ecuador (UCE). We come from software, health sciences, geology, electronics, and biotechnology. We share a belief that knowledge should be freely accessible, and we drew inspiration from EPN’s motto, “Science in the service of humanity.” Sachatellite is the result of bringing those disciplines together to make satellite data more accessible to the people who can use it.

(DEMO NOTE).- The final scene with the firefighters illustrates our long-term vision for Sachatellite: helping fire response teams act sooner. Today, the app uses historical satellite observations to identify periods that warrant closer monitoring. Our next step is to explore how combining those historical patterns with recent satellite observations could flag unusual activity and help responders prioritize which areas to investigate.
